texts.preamble: Smt.Soni Vasudev Vikram @ Soni Vikram vs M/S Mmc Enterprises on 14 September, 2022 1 Com.O.S.No.331/2021 In the Court of Lxxxiv Addl. City Civil and Sessions Judge (Cch-85 Commercial Court) Bengaluru Dated this the 14th day of September 2022 Present : Smt.H.R.Radha, B.A.L., L.L.M. Lxxxiv Addl. City Civil and Sessions Judge, (Cch-85 - Commercial Court) Bengaluru Com.O.S.No.331/2021 Plaintiff Smt.Soni Vasudev Vikram @ Soni Vikram, aged about 49 years, W/o Sri.Vikram T.S., R/at No.8, 1st floor, 6th 'C' Main, 4th Block, Jayanagar, Bengaluru - 560 011 (By Sri.G.R.Ananthram, Advocate)
texts.facts: This is a suit for ejectment of the defendants from the suit schedule property ('the premises' for short) and its vacant possession; arrears of rent of Rs.48,00,000/-, GST of Rs.69,000/- and damages of Rs.22,90,000/- upto the date of suit; arrears of electricity and water consumption charges of Rs.5,883/-; future damages at Rs.6,00,000/- p.m.; for direction to pay electricity and water consumption charges; and permanent injunction to restrain them from sub letting or carrying out interior alterations, additions and structural modifications. 2. The plaintiff's case in brief is that the 1 st defendant, represented by its partners the defendants 2 to 4, which took the premises on lease for commercial purpose under the Lease Deed dated 17.12.2018 to run a restaurant has put up temporary structure therein. The defendants are irregular in payment of rent; cheques dated 12.10.2019 and 11.11.2019 issued towards rent were dishonoured for insufficient funds. The rent for February 2020 was paid in six installments during September 2020 and rent for March 2020 was paid in part in four installments of Rs.1,00,000/- each on 06.10.2020, 08.10.2020, 09.10.2020 and 17.10.2020. GST of Rs.69,000/- for March 2020 is not paid. Owing to the defendants' default in payment of electrical consumption charges, BESCOM disconnected the power supply to the premises and she has paid Rs.5,883/- towards minimum charges to avoid removal of the meter. After receiving the legal notice dated 23.10.2020 issued in terms of clause 4(g) of the lease deed calling upon the defendants to pay the arrears within two months on 27.10.2020, only a sum of Rs.2,00,000/- was paid by NEFT on 30.10.2020. Instead of complying with the demand made in the legal notice, the defendants belatedly issued an untenable reply on 06.01.2021. She has also issued notice dated 16.12.2020 demanding remittance of arrears of TDS to Income Tax department. 2(a). The defendants 2 to 4 are responsible for the day to day conduct of 1st defendant's business and are jointly and severally liable for the dues with interest at 1.5%. The defendants are trying to induct third parties into the premises and to alter the interiors, make additions and structural modifications in order to damage the property and to harass her. The 1 st defendant's tenancy under the lease deed stood terminated for non payment of arrears of rent and defendants 2 to 4 have forfeited their tenancy rights U/s 108(l) and (q), 111(g) and (h) of the Transfer of Property Act. Despite termination of tenancy, the defendants have failed to quit and surrender vacant possession of the premises and therefore, are liable to pay damages at Rs.12,00,000/- p.m. for unauthorized possession. However, she is restricting the same to Rs.6,00,000/- p.m. The defendants are bound to pay future monthly electricity and water consumption charges upto the date of delivering vacant possession and interest at 18% p.a. 3. The defendants 1 and 2 have filed common written statement admitting that the 1st defendant, a partnership firm formed under registered Partnership Deed dated 01.11.2018 with defendants 2 to 4 as partners took the premises on lease under registered Lease Deed dated 17.12.2018 for nine years period but, deny all other allegations. It is their specific contention that there was a 55 to 60 years old house in the plaintiff's property. The rain water used to stagnate in the vacant land leased in their favour as it was at a lower level and stones were also stored there. As such they spent Rs.3 to 4 lakh to remove the stones and to raise the height of the vacant land by 3 feet using soil and have put Smt.Soni Vasudev Vikram @ Soni Vikram vs M/S Mmc Enterprises on 14 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145966786/ 3 up a temporary structure. They also changed the flooring of the entire premises with tiles, granite and marble, the electrical wiring etc., and gave it a new look by investing a huge amount in order to set up the business. The plaintiff having promised to provide cover for the three coconut trees in the premises, failed. When the POP work was going on, fronds from the coconut trees fell causing damage to major portion of the roof and the electrical wiring. As a result, they could not start the business in March 2019. It took another three months for them to complete the interior work. They have put up an MS structure at the cost of approximately Rs.15,00,000/- to provide cover for the three coconut trees and to avoid further damage. 3(a). That the plaintiff failed to provide permanent electricity connection of 40KV to run the restaurant business. Electric and electronic equipment in the premises were damaged due to temporary connection and power fluctuation, resulting in huge loss. As such they are forced to use diesel generator since March 2020 by spending more than Rs.5,00,000/- and thereby incurring loss of Rs.4,50,000/- every month and the plaintiff is liable to compensate for the same. It is at the insistence of the plaintiff that they put up the temporary structure and opted for Liquid off Take Gas System to run the business at the cost of more than Rs.3,00,000/- and by wasting 250 Sq.ft to keep the same. The plaintiff also forced them to pay Prorata charges of Rs.4,69,718/- to BWSSB to get water supply and sanitary connection and they even spent additional Rs.40,000/- to get the work done. They were also forced to spend on bore well. There is severe leakage from the plaintiff's residence in the first floor and she has failed to address the issue; and the same has damaged their reputation as well as business. Further, the lock down imposed to curb the spread of Covid-19 pandemic also resulted in huge loss. They have paid taxes to the concerned authority and also BWSSB charges to run the business legally. They have invested more than Rupees One crore to start the business but the plaintiff has failed to provide the basic facilities. They are not defaulters and have paid rents upto March 2020. 4. The defendants 3 and 4 have filed separate written statements admitting the plaint averments in para 3 and 4 that the plaintiff is the absolute owner of the premises. It was leased in favour of the 1st defendant for commercial purpose under Lease Deed dated 17.12.2018. They put up a temporary structure and are running restaurant by name Ashok Vattika. The rent was payable by the 5 th of every month and rent free period was extended at their request upto end of April 2018 but denying all other allegations. It is their specific contention that, they had tendered resignation by letter dated 10.08.2019 by the time the plaintiff presented the cheques for encashment and are absolved from all liabilities of the Firm. Subsequently, there was an agreement between them and the 2nd defendant whereby the 2nd defendant agreed to be solely responsible for all the liabilities arising out of the Firm. They have not received legal notice terminating the tenancy. After tendering resignation, they have not signed any document, particularly the postal acknowledgment. 5. At the stage of admission and denial of documents U/O XI Rule 4 CPC, as amended by Sec.16 of the Commercial Courts Act, Ex.P1 to P6 are marked for the plaintiff and Ex.D1 to D3 for the defendants. 6. Based on the pleadings, this court has framed the following: Smt.Soni Vasudev Vikram @ Soni Vikram vs M/S Mmc Enterprises on 14 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145966786/ 4 ISSUES 1. The plaintiff is examined as Pw1; she has filed affidavit in lieu of examination in chief and got marked Ex.P7 to P116, P116(a) to 116(m), P117 and P118. On behalf of the defendants, the 4 th and 2nd defendant are examined as Dw1 and Dw2 respectively; they have filed affidavits in lieu of examination in chief. During cross examination, the plaintiff confronted and got marked Ex.D4(a), Ex.P119 to P127 through Dw1 and Ex.D3(a), D9(a), D17, P117(a) to 117(c) through Dw2. While the ground floor and the vacant space attached to it are leased in favour of the defendants for running the restaurant, the plaintiff lives with her family in the First floor. Ex . P1 and P2, Khata certificate and Khata Extract show that this property which is assessed for both residential and non residential user stands in the plaintiff's name. 12. Ex. P3 is the certified copy of the Lease Deed dated 17.12.2018 entered into by and between the plaintiff and the defendants; Ex.D3 is the photocopy and Ex.D3(a) is the original registered lease deed. Ex.P4 is the certified copy of the Certificate of Registration of the 1st defendant; Ex.D7 is the original registered Partnership Deed whereas Ex.P5 is its certified copy. 13. As seen from the recitals in the Lease Deed the 1st defendant, a registered partnership firm which is in the business of hotel / restaurant took the premises on lease to have and to operate a restaurant for nine years from 15.12.2018 to 14.12.2027. Though the monthly rental was payable by 20th of every Gregorian calendar month as per clause 3(a) of the lease deed, there is no dispute that the parties mutually agreed that it should be paid by 5 th of every month; and the rent holiday from 15.12.2018 to 14.03.2019 was extended upto the end of April 2019 at the defendants' request. 15. Ex.P7 to P17 are the invoices for rent raised by the plaintiff. Ex. P19 is the office copy of the plaintiff's legal notice dated 23.10.2020 demanding arrears of rent from March 2020 within two months from the date of receipt of notice and terminating the tenancy in the event of failure to Smt.Soni Vasudev Vikram @ Soni Vikram vs M/S Mmc Enterprises on 14 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145966786/ 6 comply with the same . Ex.D1 is a copy of the notice and Ex.D1(a) is the notice served on the 1st defendant. Pw1 admits that TDS upto March 2020 and GST of Rs.69,000/- has been paid by the defendants. 16. Dw2 though admits that the rents are not paid to the plaintiff claims that only a sum of Rs.30,00,000/- was due towards the same from April 2020 to September 2020. The entries in Ex.P116 show that Rs.1,00,000/- each was paid on 06.10.2020, 08.10.2020, 09.10.2020 and 17.10.2020 towards part payment of rent for March 2020 and the balance of Rs.2,00,000/- was paid on 30.10.2020. Dw2 admits in unequivocal terms that he transferred Rs.2,00,000/- as per Ex.P116(m) only after receiving the plaintiff's notice. 17. It is not the case of the defendants' that they have paid the agreed rent @ Rs.6,00,000/- p.m. from April 2020 or December 2020. Ex.P6 dated 06.01.2021 is the 1 st defendant's reply to the plaintiff's legal notice, Ex.P19 and Dw2 admits that no payments are made thereafter. But the entries in the plaintiff's statement of account's extract Ex.P116 shows that the rent for May 2019 was paid only on 12.06.2019; and Rs.4,90,000/- was paid on 17.07.2019 and Rs.5,40,000/- each on 12.09.2019, 18.10.2019, and 16.12.2019. 52.
texts.arguments: 14. Drawing the attention to the entries in the statement of accounts at Ex.P116, the learned counsel for the plaintiff argues that the defendants were irregular in paying the rents and are in arrears of the same amounting to Rs.48,00,000/- upto the date of suit at the rate of Rs.6,00,000/- p.m. He however, fairly submits that GST of Rs.69,000/- for the month of March 2020 was paid after filing this suit. Thus, it is clear that the defendants are in arrears of rent of Rs.6,00,000/- p.m. from April to December 2020. 18. The learned counsel for the defendants 1 and 2 concedes during arguments that the defendants are in arrears of rent of Rs.48,00,000/- upto the date of suit but, submits that the plaintiff's failure to provide permanent power connection and the lock down imposed to curb Covid 19 resulted in loss to the defendants and therefore they could not pay the rents. 19. The defendants 1 and 2 too specifically contend in the written statement that they need 40KV power supply but the plaintiff did not provide the same, as such the rent was not paid. 20. Pw1 denies that the premises has temporary power connection and insists that there was commercial electricity connection to the premises since 2002. The defendants have not chosen to deny the same. The claim of Pw1 stands proved from Dw2's admission that 1SH591 is the RR number of the electricity meter relating to the premises leased in their favour and it has sanctioned power load of 20KV since inception. 21. Further, when Ex.P96 and P97 were confronted, Dw2 admits in clear terms that 4521 and 3436 units of power was consumed by them during September and October 2020 respectively. That apart, on the 2nd defendant's request the plaintiff even addressed a letter to BESCOM for renewal of electricity connection on a monthly basis, as elicited by the defendants themselves during her cross examination. This suggestion runs counter to the defendants 1 and 2's case that the plaintiff did not heed to their request in relation to power supply requirements. 30. Clause 3(a) of Ex.P3 provides that any default in payment of rent shall be a serious violation of the agreement conferring the plaintiff, the right to enter the premises and take possession. But as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the plaintiff, proof of sub letting is difficult and the same has to be gathered from the surrounding circumstances. 40. When the 1st defendant firm represented by its partners defendants 2 to 4 is admittedly running a restaurant by name 'Ashok Vattika' in the premises, the photographs at Ex.P80 and P81 show that 'Khatta Meeta Palace and Murali Pan shop' are in existence in the premises. Smt.Soni Vasudev Vikram @ Soni Vikram vs M/S Mmc Enterprises on 14 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145966786/ 11 payable by the plaintiff to get water supply and sanitation facility to the premises is paid to BWSSB by the defendants. The learned counsel for the defendants 3 and 4 vehemently argues that the said defendants cannot be made liable for the dues of the firm as they had tendered resignation long before the rents fell due; the 2 nd defendant alone was carrying on the restaurant business as the proprietor and therefore, there cannot be any decree against defendants 3 and 4. 59. Per contra, the learned counsel for the plaintiff argues that defendants 3 and 4 had not given notice of their resignation either to the plaintiff or the public in terms of Sec.72 of Indian Partnership Act and therefore the liability of principal of holding out U/s 32(3) of the Act gets attracted and each partner shall be personally held liable for the debts of the partnership firm as provided U/s 25 of the Indian Partnership Act. Under such circumstances, the judgment in Erach F.D. Mehta Vs Minoo F.D. Mehta, reported in (1970) 2 SCC 724 is not applicable to this case. 73. The learned counsel for the defendants 3 and 4 relies on the judgment in Pamuru Vishnu Vinodh Reddy Vs Chillakuru Chandrasekhara Reddy & Ors., reported in (2003) 3 SCC 445 to contend that when a partner withdraws from the Firm by dissolving it, it severs the partnership between the retiring partner and continuing partner and the defendants 3 and 4 cannot be made responsible for the dues of the firm. Smt.Soni Vasudev Vikram @ Soni Vikram vs M/S Mmc Enterprises on 14 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145966786/ 14 74. The Hon'ble Supreme Court considered the question as to which is the relevant date for ascertaining the value of the plaintiff's share in the Firm and not the effect of not issuing notice as contemplated U/s 32(3) of the Indian Partnership Act. Each partner is personally liable for debt of the Partnership Firm as held in Ashutosh Vs State of Rajasthan & Ors. reported in (2005) 7 SCC 308. 76.
